name: David Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm David, 43, and I drive a haul truck at the large mine beyond the ring road. Before the six o'clock start I walk around the tyres, check the brake sheet, then move loads between the face and the crusher; I like the quiet concentration of a clean run. Waiting for a blocked ramp can make a short shift feel long. My partner Amira works at a bakery, our two children are still in school, and the mortgage is the bill I mark first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my shift that a bit of computer help with paperwork is fine if it leaves the haul trucks running. I once used an AI chat tool to untangle a manual's warning code, then checked the actual book before touching the panel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job looks steady under this picture, yet our money is not steady. I am on the lower pay band and my partner Amira's bakery hours change with orders; one missed truck shift would eat most of the cash we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the six o'clock truck shift and check the printed manual against any AI answer. In the first year of minor changes I'd move forty from each full weekly pay packet into a separate repair account, because the car needs tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can live with a useful tool, but I do not feel relaxed about the bank balance. The truck may be sound while our old car and mortgage pull the other way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the book if the chat tool gave you the code?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A made-up code could shut down a truck or hurt someone. My foreman signs the safety sheet, but I sit in the cab when the machine starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Amira loses a bakery shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We skip the Saturday takeaway and keep the car repair money untouched if we can. My daughter notices when we cancel the takeaway, which is harder than the arithmetic.

I would **check the manual** before acting on an AI answer.
think: I see **variable wages** at home even with a steady truck job.
I know a missed shift would consume most of our **cash reserve**.
do: Keep the **six o’clock shift** and verify AI answers against the manual.
Move **forty** from full weekly pay into a car repair account.
feel: **Wary** about household money, despite modest technology change.
S0.quote: The truck may be sound while our old car and mortgage pull the other way.
fieldNote: David has **occasional AI experience**, but his safety habit is to verify answers in the printed manual.
His **thin reserve** and Amira’s variable bakery hours make ordinary bills troublesome even under a plateau.

steps.text: Keep the six o’clock truck shift and verify AI answers in the manual
Move forty from each full weekly wage to the car repair account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch will probably become quicker, but someone must still drive the trucks through the cut. I would ask the mine to show operators what the new route screen gets wrong before it becomes the only map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have seen the office leave a planner's chair empty after a resignation, and this sounds like more of that. My own hours could shrink if tighter schedules move the same rock with fewer trucks, while Amira might face automated bakery ordering as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the route-screen demonstration next month, then compare its suggested trips with my own log for a week. If the schedules actually shorten shifts in the first year, I'd ask for cross-shift truck cover and pause the kitchen repaint until the income settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about better routes and nervous about who keeps the saved hours. I can learn a screen once someone proves it works, but I can't turn a shorter rota into a full mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof that the screen helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must show the steep bend and the times when the road is slick after rain. I would try it beside the old paper log before taking a loaded truck on its suggested shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to if the shifts shorten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would speak to my supervisor Nikhil about covering an early shift on the other crew. Nikhil sets our rota, though he cannot promise the mine will keep the same number of trucks.

say: I would say **dispatch** may improve while operators still drive trucks.
I would ask for a **real route test** before dropping paper logs.
think: I suspect **shorter rotas** could cut my income.
I worry automated ordering could also reduce Amira’s **bakery hours**.
do: Compare the **route screen** with one week of truck logs.
Ask for **cross-shift cover** if schedules shorten.
Pause the **kitchen repaint** until wages settle.
feel: **Curious** about routes and nervous about saved hours.
S1.quote: I can learn a screen once someone proves it works, but I can't turn a shorter rota into a full mortgage payment.
fieldNote: David is willing to **test dispatch** against road conditions he knows from the cab.
His private fear concerns **paid hours**, including Amira’s bakery work, more than immediate truck replacement.

steps.text: Compare route-screen trips with a week of truck logs
Ask supervisor Nikhil for cross-shift truck cover if hours shorten

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI by 2028 may replace route planning first, with driverless mine trucks possible around 2031. I would ask for a written plan for the trucks, not a promise that every driver can become a technician overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work is a small slice of my day, so I might still drive after 2028. Three years later is the trouble: if robots handle the cab, I expect a large cut in drivers, and there are few similar jobs close to our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the maintenance lead this winter which electrical checks a truck operator is allowed to learn, and I'd register for the mine's paid equipment course if it opens. In 2029 I'd still drive, but I'd apply for a trainee plant-maintenance role if one is posted, even if it means a different shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be awake thinking about the mortgage and two school children when the driverless trucks arrive. I can take a course, but I cannot make a vacancy appear by working hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the course costs money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't take an unpaid place; we have less than a month's expenses saved. Amira's bakery wages cover groceries some weeks, but not the mortgage and a training fee together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son about driving trucks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my son that driving a truck was honest work for me, but he should watch what jobs still need people when he chooses an apprenticeship. I would not tell him a machine is his enemy.

say: I would say **route planning** changes in 2028 and mine trucks could change around 2031.
I would demand a **written truck plan** before accepting training promises.
think: I expect a **large driver cut** when robots handle mine trucks.
I doubt nearby work can replace my **mortgage wage** quickly.
do: Ask the **maintenance lead** about permitted electrical checks.
Register for a **paid equipment course** if offered.
Apply for a **trainee maintenance** opening in 2029 if posted.
feel: **Sleepless worry** about mortgage payments and children’s schooling.
S2.quote: I can take a course, but I cannot make a vacancy appear by working hard.
fieldNote: David separates **2028 planning AI** from possible 2031 replacement of drivers.
He is willing to **train and apply**, but both paths depend on paid places or actual vacancies.

steps.text: Ask the maintenance lead which electrical checks operators may learn
Register for a paid equipment course if the mine offers one
Apply for a trainee plant-maintenance role in 2029 if posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to AGI gives the mine time to test dispatch properly, and robot trucks might follow around 2034. The owners should publish which cabs they plan to change and how current drivers can qualify for other paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when thinking AI arrives, I could still have truck work while my children finish school. By 51, when robots arrive, I may need a second income path, and our small savings would not carry a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the equipment demonstration this year and keep a notebook of the failures and fixes. I'd take the vocational college's evening electrical module if the fees fit our budget; in 2032 I'd ask the mine for a paid transfer to fixed plant before the trucks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The years help because I can try a course while drawing wages. I still feel a knot over paying for it if Amira's hours drop in the same month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you spend on the evening module?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to see the fee before I promised anything. We could cover a small monthly payment if the car holds together, but I won't put a course on the store card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record in that notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The route screen missing a wet bend, an incorrect payload estimate, and whether the supervisor fixed it. A notebook with dates is more useful than saying the software feels wrong.

say: I would ask owners for **cab plans** and paid paths for current drivers.
I would say **robot trucks** might follow thinking AI around 2034.
think: I may still drive at **48**, but need another income path by 51.
Our **small reserve** cannot carry a long gap in wages.
do: Record **equipment failures** during demonstrations this year.
Take an **evening electrical module** if fees fit the budget.
feel: **More able to plan**, but worried about course fees.
S3.quote: A notebook with dates is more useful than saying the software feels wrong.
fieldNote: David’s **test notebook** reflects measured openness to technology rather than blind faith in it.
An evening course is **conditional** on affordable fees, while a paid transfer would protect mortgage income.

steps.text: Record route-screen failures and fixes in a dated notebook
Take the vocational college evening electrical module if affordable
Ask for a paid fixed-plant transfer in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a 2036 thinking AI date and robot trucks around 2039 give us time to prepare, but we should use it. I would want training places tied to real jobs at the mine, not a poster about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when thinking AI arrives, I may still be on a truck; at 56, robot trucks could remove that income. The children will be adults then, but the mortgage might still exist and I cannot assume a pension will replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue driving and ask the pension office for a statement this year so I know the actual numbers. I'd put any shift premium into mortgage principal after the car tyres are paid for, then in 2037 I'd review posted maintenance jobs and apply where my skills really match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed because I can prepare in stages and keep a pay packet for now. I would still be uneasy if the mine waited until the last year to tell us how many drivers it needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in the pension statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The projected payment at 56 and the penalty for drawing it early, if there is one. I am not treating retirement as guaranteed just because the calendar has ten years on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another mine job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a real offer and a talk with Amira about her bakery work. By then the children may live elsewhere, but selling our house for a rumour would be foolish.

say: I would ask for **job-linked training** before robot trucks arrive around 2039.
I would say the **ten years** are useful only if the mine acts.
think: I may need **wages at 56**, whatever the children’s plans.
I cannot assume a **pension** covers the mortgage.
do: Put **shift premiums** toward mortgage principal after car tyres.
Review **maintenance vacancies** in 2037 and apply where qualified.
feel: **Less pressed**, though still uneasy about late employer decisions.
S4.quote: I am not treating retirement as guaranteed just because the calendar has ten years on it.
fieldNote: David considers the children’s **adult lives** rather than carrying school costs forward into 2039.
He would pay down the **mortgage** and check pension figures before relying on any retirement date.

steps.text: Request a pension statement showing payment and early-draw penalty
Put shift premiums toward mortgage principal after paying for tyres
Apply for matching mine maintenance vacancies in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robot trucks could follow in 2031 before I have a new qualification. A paid equipment course with actual maintenance vacancies behind it would help, along with a clear schedule for changing the fleet. I would use the time, but I need wages while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether operators can challenge a machine's route when the road is wet. We should still be able to stop an unsafe trip, even if a screen drew the line.

headlineQuote: We should still be able to stop an unsafe trip, even if a screen drew the line.
portrait: David is a **43-year-old haul-truck operator** with a mortgage, two school-age children and a thin cash reserve.
He sometimes uses **AI tools**, but checks them against manuals and road conditions.
He expects **planning software** before robot trucks and tests new systems with dated evidence.
He would pursue **paid training** and posted maintenance jobs while protecting household wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring robot trucks by 2031 before David gains another qualification.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid equipment course**, real maintenance vacancies and a clear fleet schedule would help David prepare.
